extraction_text: From this origin emerged the progenitor, the lord, the sole Prajapati, Brahma, the ancestor of gods, the pillar of heaven, Manu, and the supreme being.
From this emerged the Prolific race, Daksha and his seven sons, and from them came twenty-one lords of beings.
Also emerged the infinite Purusha (Cosmic Person), known to all sages, along with all gods: Adityas, Vasus, Ashvins, Yakshas, Sadhyas, Pishachas, Kushikas, and ancestors.
From this emerged knowledgeable, cultured, stainless Brahmarishis, and many royal sages possessing all virtues.

The speaker explains that everything is governed by Time (Kala), which creates, matures, destroys, and recreates all beings impartially.

attributes.action: Exposition on the nature of Time

extraction_text: The sage Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana) taught this wisdom about dharma and liberation.
Studying the Mahabharata purifies all sins, and it narrates the deeds of gods, sages, kings, and divine beings.
The text particularly narrates the divine deeds of Krishna (Vasudeva), who is described as Truth, Righteousness, Pure, Eternal, Brahman, Supreme, and Light.
The text describes the origin and nature of the universe from a divine source, encompassing concepts of reality, unreality, tradition, action, birth, death, and rebirth.

It narrates the spirit and the material world composed of the five great elements (earth, water, fire, wind, space) with their inherent qualities, and also mentions tendencies toward the 'unmanifest'.
Exceptional ascetics, devoted to practice and possessing powers of meditation and yoga, see what is within their own hearts as clearly as seeing an image in a mirror.
Those with faith, who regularly practice, revere true dharma, and study this chapter will be freed from sin.
This chapter of the Mahabharata is named the 'Introduction' (序目篇); faithful people who constantly listen to it from the beginning will not fall into difficulties.
Reciting part of this 'Introduction' at dawn and dusk instantly absolves sins committed during the day and night.
The Mahabharata itself is described as truth, immortal nectar; like ghee in curd, like a Brahmin among two-legged beings.
As the ocean is supreme among waters and the cow is best among four-legged beings, so too is the Mahabharata supreme.
If someone recites a single verse from it to Brahmins during ancestral rites, the food offered to ancestors will endure forever.
The Vedas are expanded through historical texts and Puranas; the Vedas fear the less knowledgeable, lest they be misunderstood.
A scholar who recites this 'Black Sage Veda' (Mahabharata) and understands its meaning will destroy even the sin of killing a fetus, without doubt.
A pure person who recites this chapter on each lunar phase change (new moon, full moon, first quarter, last quarter) is considered to have studied the entire Mahabharata.
One who recites this sage's book with faith regularly will obtain long life, fame, and ascend to heaven.
The four Vedas were placed on one side of a balance and the Mahabharata on the other by gods and sages; the Mahabharata was greater and heavier, hence called the 'Great' (Maha) Bharata.
One who knows its meaning eliminates all sins.
Austerity is not a sin, studying the Vedas is not a sin, natural Vedic rituals are not a sin, taking wealth by force is not a sin; only when their nature is destroyed do these become sins.
The text defines the four varnas (social classes) of ancient India: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors/rulers), Vaishyas (merchants/farmers), and Shudras (laborers).
The text describes the Puranas as a class of ancient Indian texts compiled over centuries, containing mythology, religion, and royal genealogies.
The text defines Dharma as the code of conduct prescribed by Brahmanism, including religious rituals.
The Vedas are described as sacred collections of ancient knowledge compiled by Brahmin priests into four texts.
The text explains Brahman as the cosmic spirit in Indian idealist philosophy.
Indian mythology divides the world into three or more realms (underground, earth, heaven).
The text describes the four Yugas (ages): Satya Yuga, Treta Yuga, Dvapara Yuga, and Kali Yuga, which degrade over time until world destruction.
Various mythological beings are defined: Yakshas (minor deities/demons), Gandharvas (celestial musicians), Rakshasas (demons), and others.
The text mentions Yoga as physical and mental discipline, and the three aims of life: Dharma (duty), Artha (wealth), and Kama (desire).
